gap:S16.model_size_notes:
Opus: the skill made no real difference. Criterion scores were identical ([1,1,1,1] for both); one judge gave the skill a slight edge, the other a tie. The skill reply's extra value was framing: A is dominated, flipping quality's sign doesn't change the winner, and the dollar threshold for B vs C. I re-checked all of it as correct. The difference is within one-sample noise. At 235 words it ran past the Standard target of 180 or fewer, but judges did not penalize that.

Sonnet: S16 has no sonnet data, so no conclusion is possible.

Haiku: the skill was clearly worse in this sample (both judges, clear margins). The cause was one comparison slip ('C wins' when B scored 956 and C 1,107) in an extra calculation the skill encouraged, plus a recommendation against B ('I would not pick B on this formula alone') written before the supporting numbers. Baseline haiku (84 words) did less and made no errors. Skill haiku (127 words) tried more and got the one part beyond the baseline wrong.

The pattern: at small sizes, the skill's push toward verdicts, labeled alternatives and reversal checks gives more chances for error unless it is paired with an explicit recompute and consistency check. A verdict-first layout also lets a model without hidden reasoning commit to a conclusion before computing it. The fixes proposed above target exactly this and do not remove the behavior that worked on opus. With one sample per cell, the haiku slip itself may be noise, but the missing check is a real gap and cheap to close.

gap:S16.verdict:
The net effect was neutral on opus (a slight, correct analytical gain within noise) and negative on haiku, where one wrong 'C wins' claim under a labeled correction decided the pair. There is no sonnet data.

On rubric criteria 1-3 (faithful arithmetic, the backwards quality term, dollar dominance) the skill added nothing measurable, because both baselines already got them at both sizes. The skill's real contribution is pushing toward criterion 4 (a labeled alternative plus whether the winner changes) and threshold framing. Opus did this well; haiku did it wrong, and the skill has no step that would catch the error.

Minimal edits, in priority order:
1. Add 'every stated total, ranking, and winner recomputed and consistent with the stated direction and with your other claims' to the core's final check.
2. Put a one-sentence supplied-formula rule in core §6.4: apply as written and report first; flag direction and unit problems; compute any labeled correction in full and say whether its winner differs, where an unchanged winner is a valid finding. Also add formula- or score-based decisions to the edge-case pointer.
3. In §7, when the user asks to apply their method, the verdict is that method's result, and any recommendation of the model's own goes after the numbers that support it.

These edits keep the behavior that worked on opus and target the haiku failure directly. Caveat: one sample per cell, so the haiku slip may partly be noise, but the missing verification step is a real, checkable gap in the text.
